summary: Describes a straightforward format for writing concise yet descriptive MIB modules used in network management. It is an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1212 defines a compact way to describe objects in a Management Information Base (MIB) for network management. Its extended OBJECT-TYPE macro combines an object's formal properties and descriptive text in one definition. The memo says future MIB modules are intended to use this format.

subtitle: A compact ASN.1 format that puts each managed object's definition in one place.

tldr.problem: MIB objects were described in both prose and formal definitions, creating duplicated information that could become inconsistent.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1212 extends the ASN.1 OBJECT-TYPE macro with clauses for syntax, access, status, description, references, row indexes and default values.
tldr.outcome: The memo intends all future MIB modules to use this concise format. It is an Internet Standard.

today: RFC 1212 is an Internet Standard. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the memo states that future MIB modules are intended to use this format.

sections.title: Why a More Concise MIB Format Was Needed
sections.content:
The Internet management framework used the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), a Structure of Management Information (SMI), and a Management Information Base (MIB). As more objects were added, their MIB descriptions repeated information in separate textual and formal definitions.

RFC 1212 proposes an enhancement that removes this duplication while retaining descriptive information. It says the resulting concise format is intended for all future MIB modules.
sections.plainLanguage: MIB object definitions repeated information in prose and in formal notation. This memo combines those descriptions so authors can state an object's details once.

sections.title: Tables and Column Objects
sections.content:
SNMP operations apply to scalar objects. Developers often arrange these objects in conceptual tables, with rows made from scalar columnar objects. The table and row are defined with OBJECT-TYPE, using the ACCESS value not-accessible.

Rows are a convention for people and management applications, not a structure enforced by the protocol. For example, a Get-Next operation at the last column in a row continues to the next object instance rather than returning an error. A row can be invalidated by setting its status object, but whether an agent removes it is implementation-specific.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB table is an arrangement that helps people understand a list of objects. SNMP itself handles the objects in order and does not enforce rows.

sections.title: How an Agent May Add a Row
sections.content:
A management station can request new object instances with an SNMP set operation. When an instance does not yet exist, the agent may reject the request with noSuchName, create the requested instances and reject unsuitable values with badValue, or create the requested instances plus other instances needed to complete a row.

The RFC says all three behaviors conform to SNMP, subject to access control and the definitions of the objects. An agent's behavior is therefore not fixed to one row-creation method by this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: When asked to create a row, an agent may refuse, create only the requested objects, or create those objects and fill out the row. The memo treats all three choices as conformant.

sections.title: The Extended OBJECT-TYPE Definition
sections.content:
The extended OBJECT-TYPE macro combines the textual and formal parts of an object definition. SYNTAX, ACCESS and STATUS are required. Syntax describes the object's data structure using a restricted subset of ASN.1; access states the minimum required level of support; and status states the required implementation support.

DESCRIPTION and REFERENCE are optional clauses, although DESCRIPTION is required if the module has no other textual description. INDEX identifies a conceptual row, and DEFVAL supplies an acceptable default an agent may use when creating an instance. The macro's value is the object's name, an object identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Each object definition has required fields for its data type, access and support status. It can also include a description, a reference, a row index or a default value.

sections.title: How INDEX Identifies Rows
sections.content:
The INDEX clause appears on an object representing a conceptual row. It names the object values that distinguish one row from another. If a non-columnar object has no INDEX clause, its instance identifier is the object name followed by a sub-identifier of zero.

Index syntax determines how values become sub-identifiers: an integer contributes its value; a fixed-length string contributes one sub-identifier per octet; and variable-length strings and object identifiers include a length followed by their components. An IpAddress contributes four sub-identifiers. DEFVAL may provide a value for a column omitted from a row-creation request. If no acceptable default exists, the indexed objects must be read-write.
sections.plainLanguage: An INDEX clause names the values that distinguish one row from another. The data type of each value determines how it is represented in the object's identifier.

sections.title: Example: The IP Address Translation Table
sections.content:
The memo shows how to define the MIB-II ipNetToMediaTable with the extended macro. The table maps IP addresses to physical addresses. Its row uses an INDEX made from the interface index and network address; the row definition also lists the columns that describe each entry.

The example's type column can be set to invalid(2) to invalidate a mapping. Whether the agent removes an invalidated entry remains implementation-specific, so a manager must inspect the type column when interpreting table entries.
sections.plainLanguage: The worked example defines a table that maps IP addresses to physical addresses. It shows how the table, its row index and its columns fit into the combined definition.

sections.title: Converting Other MIB Definitions
sections.content:
The appendix describes converting MIBs from other organizations into the Internet-standard format. It recommends grouping objects by conformance, where an implementation supports all objects in a group or none, and starting with a core set of essential objects.

Objects that can have multiple instances become conceptual tables. A row should contain no more than approximately 20 objects as a rule of thumb, so it can fit in one PDU. The appendix also describes mappings for syntax types and says actions are represented as read-write objects whose written value triggers the action.
sections.plainLanguage: To convert another organization's MIB, group related objects and map each object's type and behavior into this format. The memo suggests keeping rows small enough to fit in one PDU.
